source.title: What the State Owes
source.summary: Government spending, public goods provision, and the dual model of bayt al-mal and waqf.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: Once you collect taxes, how do you spend them? This episode examines government spending categories (defense, infrastructure, education, healthcare, transfers), the efficiency arguments for and against public provision, and the problems of bureaucracy, crowding out, and rent-seeking. The Islamic historical record shows a dual model: the bayt al-mal funded defense, infrastructure, and poverty relief directly, while the waqf system created a parallel, voluntary layer of public goods provision including hospitals, schools, and water infrastructure. Neither was perfect. The waqf system suffered from rigidity and eventual state capture under the Ottomans. But the institutional design, combining state and non-state provision, is worth studying on its own terms.

thread: The Ottomans ran two parallel systems for public goods. The bayt al-mal handled defense and infrastructure through taxes. The waqf system funded hospitals and schools through voluntary donations.
You paid taxes for roads and armies. You donated to waqfs for everything else. Hospitals, schools, water systems — all funded by voluntary endowments that lasted centuries.
The waqf system created something government spending couldn't: permanent funding streams that survived political changes. A single endowment could fund a hospital for 500 years.

Both systems had flaws. Waqfs became rigid over time. The state eventually captured them. But the dual model separated forced from voluntary provision in ways worth studying. https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-trt-3

linkedin.post: Public goods provision doesn't have to be a binary choice between state and market. The Ottoman Empire demonstrated a sophisticated dual model that modern economists are rediscovering. The bayt al-mal (state treasury) funded defense, infrastructure, and poverty relief through taxation. Meanwhile, the waqf system created a parallel layer of voluntary public goods provision — hospitals, schools, water infrastructure — funded by religious endowments. Neither system was perfect. Waqfs eventually became rigid and suffered state capture. But the institutional design is fascinating: combining mandatory and voluntary provision, creating funding streams that could last centuries while separating different types of public goods. This historical model offers insights for contemporary debates about government spending, crowding out effects, and the role of civil society in providing public goods. Listen: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-trt-3

instagram.caption: The Ottoman Empire solved public goods provision with a brilliant dual system most economists have never heard of. The bayt al-mal (state treasury) handled the basics: defense, infrastructure, poverty relief. Funded by taxes, managed by government. The waqf system ran parallel: hospitals, schools, water systems. Funded by voluntary religious endowments, managed by trustees. You paid taxes for roads and armies. You donated to waqfs for everything else. The genius? Waqf endowments created permanent funding streams. A single donation could fund a hospital for 500 years, surviving political changes that would kill government programs. Both systems had flaws. Waqfs became rigid over time. The state eventually captured them. But the institutional design separated forced from voluntary provision in ways worth studying. Modern debates about government spending vs private provision miss this historical model entirely.
